title: Butterman
materials: fiberglass, steel plate, light and sound device, 2026
exhibitions: Migratory Birds 300- Public Art Section, Aranya Resort, Hebei, China, June, 2026
Fantasy Carnival, Shanghai, China, April 30-May 5, 2026
statement:
Inspired by interactive educational toys, the work explores how toys shape children’s cognition and behavior. Toys are not neutral objects; they enter children’s worlds through processes of production, design, and selection. 

Seven buttons on the work’s wings activate lights and sounds when pressed, translating a familiar mechanism of play into an embodied experience. This seemingly simple “press–response” structure cultivates a reliance on rules, efficiency, and immediate feedback through repeated interaction. Toys are more than objects of play; they shape how we play, how we respond, and ultimately, who we become within society.

statement: In this work, a transparent sandcastle melting by the sea becomes a metaphor for the gradual disappearance of childhood. Set against a culture in which childhood is increasingly adultified while adults long for lost innocence, the work reflects on growth, loss, and the reconstruction of the self.

exhibitions: Technically Sweet, RISD Tap Room, Rhode Island, United States, October 5, 2026.
statement: The animation examines how advertising, cartoons, and television shape children’s self-image and expectations of adulthood. The childhood dream of becoming a hero gives way to earning a living by impersonating one in Times Square. Juxtaposing heroic narratives with the labor of performance, the work considers how mass media packages aspirations into images to identify with, which individuals later perform for income. Childhood’s promises do not disappear; they are repriced within the economic realities of adulthood.

title: GNOMES
exhibitions: Technically Sweet, RISD Tap Room, Rhode Island, United States, October 5, 2026.
statement:
Taking the garden gnome as its protagonist, the work explores the relationship between marginal identity, cultivation, and growth. The gnome moves between an elemental being associated with the underworld, a figure in fairy tales such as Snow White, and a commodified ornament placed in a garden. Across these shifting identities, an autonomous being becomes an object to be named, shaped, and positioned.

The garden becomes a space in which growth is deliberately organized: life is nurtured, but also pruned, classified, and disciplined. Through the gnome’s movement between myth, fairy tale, and commodity, the work asks how growth is shaped by external expectations, and how an individual might find possibilities for existence beyond an assigned place.

title: WordyGnome
statement:
This work grew out of a confusion I experienced while learning English as a child. The definitions I learned from textbooks often felt very different from the ways those same words were actually used in everyday life. A seemingly simple word could carry completely different implications, emotions, and judgments depending on its context.

The work explores the gap between denotation and connotation, and how we learn, understand, and use language. Language is never neutral. As culture and social contexts shift, words acquire new meanings. Rather than searching for the correct meaning of each word, this work focuses on the unstable distance between definition and use, and on what that distance can reveal about the culture in which language exists.

statement: Through fabric and the form of hopscotch, the work explores childhood as a social construct. Rather than originating as a children’s game, hopscotch began as a military exercise designed to regulate soldiers’ bodies and movements. From children regarded as “miniature adults” in ancient Greece and Rome to the disciplining of bodies and behavior throughout contemporary childhood, the boundaries between childhood and adulthood are becoming increasingly blurred.

materials: Fabric, found children's clothes, beads, found toys, wood, 2025
statement: The work uses secondhand children’s clothing, fabric, toys, and beads within a wooden frame, creating a compressed structure in which soft materials are forced to form boundaries. Rather than being predetermined, these boundaries emerge through density, exclusion, and the occupation of space. Western jigsaw puzzles originated as dissected maps, carrying colonial visions of the world and forms of geopolitical instruction rooted in violence. Through repeated play from an early age, children learn to assemble the world as discrete, bounded territories, shaping how they come to understand its geography and political order. Drawing on this imagery, the work shifts attention to how boundaries are produced, rather than existing naturally, they are learned, internalized, and normalized through compression, division, and exclusion.
